passage:
Subject: Thursday's client pitch

Hi Ujjwal,
I wanted to write this instead of saying it in the corridor. This morning you mentioned your migraine is back and that you're "drowning" in the vendor files, so the pitch may be rough. I noticed you said something similar before the March review and before the budget meeting. I'm not saying you aren't tired or unwell; only you know that. I just wonder if these big presentations feel heavier than they need to.
So, for what it's worth: nobody on this team needs the pitch to be perfect. Your slides in March were clear, and the client asked you the follow-up questions, not me. If Thursday is a bit messy, it's still your work, and we'll learn from it together. If you like, we can do a dry run Wednesday at five.
Parveen

qa.q: When had Ujjwal said something similar before?
qa.a: Before the March review and before the budget meeting.

qa.q: What is Parveen thinking about why Ujjwal mentions the migraine and the vendor files?
qa.a: Parveen wonders whether the big presentations feel too heavy, and whether warning that the pitch may be rough gives Ujjwal a cushion in case it isn't perfect.

qa.q: Which part of Parveen's email gives Ujjwal the most useful choice?
qa.a: The offer of a dry run on Wednesday at five lets Ujjwal prepare with support, so full effort feels safer than an early excuse.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal feel reading that the pitch doesn't need to be perfect?
qa.a: Ujjwal may feel noticed and a little exposed, but also relieved that a messy Thursday won't cost the team's respect 🙂.

grounding: A colleague notices a teammate's pre-presentation illness and overload pattern and writes to reassure that effort and imperfection are welcome.

passage: You asked what I've learned as a team lead this year? One thing, about Hrithik. I'm Tejas, by the way, for anyone new listening. Hrithik is sharp, really sharp. But every single time we had a demo for the directors, the day before, he'd come to my desk: "Bro, my back's killing me," or "I've got three deadlines, so this might be half-baked." At first I just said, "Take it easy." By the fourth time I saw the pattern. So before the October demo I took him for chai and said, "Listen, you've never given a bad demo. And if one day it's average, that's fine. I'd rather see you try fully and stumble than hold back." He looked at his cup for ages. The next day, no warning speech. The demo wasn't perfect. It was good.

qa.q: What did Hrithik say the day before demos?
qa.a: "Bro, my back's killing me," or "I've got three deadlines, so this might be half-baked."

qa.q: What does Hrithik's long look at his cup suggest?
qa.a: It suggests the words touched something, perhaps relief or embarrassment that the pattern had been seen and that he didn't need a cushion.

qa.q: What changed when Tejas stopped saying 'Take it easy'?
qa.a: By naming the pattern kindly over chai and saying an average demo was fine, Tejas made full effort feel safe, and Hrithik dropped the warning speech.

qa.q: Why might Hrithik have needed the warning speech in the first place?
qa.a: Presenting to directors may have felt like a test of how sharp he is, so a sore back or three deadlines kept a reason ready if it went badly.

grounding: A team lead describes noticing a teammate's pre-demo excuses and reassuring him that trying fully is welcome even if imperfect.

passage: Anjali here, writing this down because I keep thinking about it. Joseph sits next to me on the hospital admin team. Before the quarterly audit presentation, he told three people he had a fever coming on. Before the one in June, it was "I haven't slept, the rota is killing me." Both times, his presentation was actually fine. I couldn't tell if he was really unwell; he might have been. But on Monday, when he started with "I'm so overloaded, don't expect much," I said, "Joseph, whatever you bring is welcome. You've prepared, and if a slide goes wrong, we'll fix it together." He blinked, laughed a little, and said, "Okay. Okay." On Wednesday he presented without any warnings first. His hands shook a bit at the start. Then they didn't.

qa.q: What did Joseph say before the quarterly audit presentation?
qa.a: He told three people he had a fever coming on.

qa.q: Why might Joseph laugh a little and say 'Okay. Okay.'?
qa.a: He may have felt caught but also relieved; hearing that his effort was welcome loosened his need for a ready excuse.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Anjali's approach?
qa.a: Instead of only sympathising, Anjali said whatever Joseph brought was welcome and slides could be fixed together, which lowered the stakes.

qa.q: What was Wednesday like for Joseph without a warning ready?
qa.a: His hands shook at first, showing it took courage to present with no cushion, and then he steadied.

grounding: A colleague notices a teammate's pattern of illness and overload before presentations and reassures him that effort is welcome.

passage:
Monday: The quarterly review was on Friday, and Francis had the second slot. At stand-up, Francis mentioned a sore throat 'coming on' and three urgent tickets. Samir remembered the same two things before the last review, and the one before that. He felt a flash of irritation: again?
Wednesday: Samir found Francis at the coffee machine. 'Throat any better?' Francis rubbed the back of the neck. 'Honestly, if the talk's rough, it's because I'm running on empty.' Samir kept his voice light. 'Nobody's expecting a perfect talk, you know. Last time your rough version still had the best numbers. I'd rather see you try it properly and trip a bit.' Francis laughed awkwardly, then went quiet.
Friday: Francis presented without mentioning the throat. One chart was wrong and got fixed live. Afterwards Francis caught Samir's eye and nodded.

qa.q: What two things did Francis mention at Monday's stand-up?
qa.a: A sore throat 'coming on' and three urgent tickets.

qa.q: What did Samir feel on noticing the pattern, and why?
qa.a: Samir felt a flash of irritation, 'again?', because the same excuses had come before the last two reviews as well.

qa.q: What choice did Samir make on Wednesday, and why did it help?
qa.a: Samir chose to reassure rather than accuse: nobody expects a perfect talk, and a real try is welcome even if it trips; that took the pressure off, so Francis presented without the throat story.

qa.q: What might Francis have been afraid of before each review?
qa.a: Francis may have feared that a weak talk would show a lack of ability; illness or workload made a poor result explainable, until Samir made imperfection feel safe.

grounding: A colleague notices a teammate always has an illness or overload ready before big presentations and reassures that effort and imperfect results are both welcome.

passage:
Jasleen, sit a minute. Twice this week you've told me you might be coming down with something before Thursday's board meeting. Let me tell you about Rakesh.
When I was twenty-five, at the insurance office in Chandigarh, Rakesh sat beside me. Clever man. And every time he had to present to the regional head, the day before there'd be a headache, or his mother visiting, or 'I've had no time at all.' I'll admit I resented it a little; I was presenting too, and I had no excuses.
Then one evening I said to him, 'Rakesh, if you try your best and it's ordinary, that's allowed. We'll still sit together at lunch.' He laughed at me: 'Alka, you sound like my mother.' But the next time, no headache. His talk was a bit dull, and he was fine.
So, Jasleen. Try fully. Ordinary is allowed.

qa.q: Where did Alka work at twenty-five?
qa.a: At the insurance office in Chandigarh.

qa.q: How did young Alka feel about Rakesh's excuses, and why?
qa.a: Alka resented them a little, because Alka was presenting too and had no excuses to lean on.

qa.q: What did Alka choose to say to Rakesh, and why did it help?
qa.a: That trying his best and being ordinary was allowed, and they would still sit together at lunch; it made an imperfect result safe, so the excuse was no longer needed.

qa.q: How might Jasleen hear this story, given the week's talk of coming down with something?
qa.a: Jasleen may feel gently caught out on recognising the pattern, but also relieved that an ordinary, honest try at Thursday's meeting would be welcome.

grounding: An elder recalls noticing a colleague's pre-presentation excuses and reassuring him that full effort with an ordinary result was welcome.
